extracted.intended_audience: Inventors, patent practitioners, and applicants preparing US design patent drawings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for preparing drawings (or photos) for U.S. design patent applications, including required views, shading, use of broken lines, and procedural steps for exceptions (color/photographs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format: black-and-white line drawings (default)
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, figures for a design patent application should be drawn in black-and-white line drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike utility patent drawings, proper surface shading must be included. The USPTO provides a guide on design patent applications. Broken lines may be used to show subject matter that does not form a part of the claimed design. In special circumstances, black-and-white photographs may be filed in lieu of ink drawings if the photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (37 CFR §1.84(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate surface shading in the drawings must clearly show the character and contour of all surfaces of any three-dimensional aspects of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface shading is also necessary to distinguish between open space and solid areas. Lack of appropriate surface shading may result in a non-enabling rejection under 35 U.S.C. §112(a) [first paragraph]. Addition of surface shading after initial filing might be considered new matter (see 35 U.S.C. §132(a)), making it difficult to resolve such rejections. Examples: straight-line shading to indicate a flat surface; stippling for curved or non-flat surfaces. The author discourages inventors from using their own drawings which often lead to examiner objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required views (head-on) and perspective views
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent drawings must show the following required views: front; rear; right side; left side; top; and bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The above required views must be shown head-on and not from an angle. Views shown from an angle, however slight, are called 'perspective views' which may be included. Perspective views are optional but helpful in showing depth and shape of three-dimensional features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting duplicate or mirror-image views (with statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Views that are merely duplicates or mirror images of other views of the design may be omitted if the specification makes this explicitly clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, if the left and right sides are identical or mirror images, provide a single view and include a statement such as 'the right side elevational view is a mirror image of the left side' in the drawing description. This explicit statement permits omission of redundant views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting bottom view when flat/unornamented (with statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bottom is flat and includes no ornamentation, that view may be omitted if the figure descriptions include a statement explaining the view (e.g., 'the bottom is flat and unornamented').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: 'Unornamented' should not be used to describe visible surfaces that clearly are not flat. Include a clear descriptive statement in the figure descriptions when omitting views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broken or dashed lines to show unclaimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines may be used to depict portions that form no part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broken or dashed lines are helpful to show context without claiming surrounding environment. Note: some foreign offices (e.g., China) do not allow broken lines; what is dashed in a US application may need to be shown as solid in foreign counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color drawings / color photographs: petition and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition must be filed if an applicant seeks to file color drawings or color photographs in lieu of black-and-white drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition under 37 CFR §1.84(a)(2) should explain why color drawings or photographs are necessary. The petition must include the petition fee (37 CFR §1.17(h)), three sets of color drawings or photographs, and the specification must contain the following language: 'The patent or application file contains at least one drawing executed in color. Copies of this patent or patent application publication with color drawing(s) will be provided by the Office upon request and payment of the necessary fee.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs vs ink drawings: when photographs allowed and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Black-and-white photographs may be filed in lieu of ink drawings only if the photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention (37 CFR §1.84(b)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photos cannot be combined with black-and-white line drawings in one design application (see MPEP 1503.02). If photographs are submitted instead of ink drawings, the photos should not show any environmental structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written disclaimers not permitted in issued design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Written disclaimer statements are not permitted in issued design patents, but are temporarily allowed in a pending design application to enable future amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, the most effective way to avoid claiming a particular design feature or element is to show such feature in broken or dashed lines rather than rely on a written disclaimer for the issued patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and procedural handling of improper drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper design patent drawings will result in an Office Action specifying the issues; a timely response with replacement drawings is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Office Action response does not adequately resolve drawing objections, a second Office Action may follow. Drawing objections can delay allowance by several months to a year or more; in some cases the application may be rejected and never allowed. Because adding shading after filing may be treated as new matter, initial compliance is critical. The article recommends submitting proper drawings upfront to avoid delays and extra expense.
